question: on winter days, does the Ti flange with its capsule make the cambium under the Ø15–Ø29.8 ring colder than under bark without it, and how does the answer move with the sky and the sun?
method: 1D implicit column on 78's grid (properties of 58) with a surface energy balance — convection, long-wave exchange with a clear (Brutsaert 1975) or overcast sky and air-temperature surroundings at sky view 0.5, and optionally ERA5 diffuse sun — over 30 ERA5 years; under the flange the balance acts through a fin of A_fin/A_contact

brutsaert.coefficient_read_via: Crawford & Duchon 1999, J. Appl. Meteor. 38:474 (open text)

forms.linear: ours — the two sky ends mixed by the cover
forms.b82: Brutsaert 1982 as printed in Herrero & Polo 2012 eq. 8, C = 0.22

verdict.text: The sign of the shift depends on the sky and the sun. Clear sky, no sun — the end most favourable to the flange: the tied median is -2.6…-0.5 K (warmer under the flange), because a long-wave deficit depresses flat bark (-6.9 K at its equilibrium) more than the capsule (-5.7 K) — with the capsule's h_c set to bark's the tied median turns +0.4 K. Overcast, no sun: +0.3…+0.6 K (colder) — the fin's conductance to the air (6× bark's) makes the ring follow the air's daily fall. Diffuse sun on both raises it again (bark banks the gain, the fin sheds it): clear -1.7…+0.1 K, overcast +1.1…+1.4 K. The worst day of the four ends is +4.6 K colder (overcast_diffuse_sun, tied). Decoupled — the flange's band alone, 0.54× the ring — moves the same way with smaller medians. Weighed by the site's real cloud (ERA5: winter median cover 0.98, above 0.8 in 72% of winter hours), the answer turns on how cover becomes sky radiation, and the one measurement in hand (a mountain station, by day) does not settle it for a valley cell at night: if full cover radiates as a black body at air temperature (the two ends mixed by the cover), the tied flange is colder on 26%–68% of frost days without sun and 69%–89% with diffuse sun (median +0.5…+1.2 K); with Brutsaert 1982's factor at its original C 0.22, which leaves a fully covered winter sky short of a black body, on 0%–36% and 11%–76%. On the cold days (bark below -10 °C), the tail an injury threshold sits in: 58%–88% colder under the first, 0%–48% under the second without sun. Beam sun on a trunk face and the real coupling are not in the tree; 1D inflates the shift in both signs. The regional injury threshold and its corrections live in canon (docs/01_04 §3.1): it sits NEAR this model's floor, not far below it.

ceilings: the sun is bracketed by its ends — beam sun on a trunk face is not computed (it needs the mounting azimuth); real cloud (ERA5) is weighed, through two long-wave forms that disagree under full cover — which one holds at the site decides the sign, and neither form's primary was read
1D and zero contact resistance inflate the shift in both signs; the tied end is the upper end of the coupling axis only, and the two coupling ends bracket the median, not the tail
the radome↔flange coupling is not measured — decoupled and tied are its two ends
F 0.5, ε 0.90, α_bark 0.80 and the trunk's convection correlation are ours; α_fin is the radome's specified ceiling and a lighter finish enlarges the shift
no injury verdict — no frost-hardiness threshold for pine cambium in the tree
absolute minima are the model's lower bound (weeks of sunless clear sky), not a forecast
snow or rime on the bark or the radome is not modelled
the lump here is fed by the bark — it is not the capsule temperature 71 gives the EDLC floor
